title: Payment Failures in Southeast Asia: The Hidden Cost Beyond Lost Sales
summary: A failed payment costs more than the sale. See the full cost of payment failures in Southeast Asia and how to detect, recover, and reconcile them faster.
body_markdown:
A


**failed payment** costs your business more than the value of the order behind it. As


**digital payments** take a larger share of commerce across Southeast Asia, every failed transaction also creates work for your support, engineering, and finance teams. That makes the real cost of payment failures higher than the revenue your business sees missing at checkout.


The frequency is higher than most businesses assume. Visa found that


[6 in 10 consumers in Asia Pacific](https://www.visa.com.sg/about-visa/stories/2025/commerce-of-tomorrow-why-ecommerce-growth-in-asia-pacific-depends-on-frictionless-secure-payments.html) experienced


**issues paying with their cards for e-commerce** in the past year, with


**14% running into problems** on more than four occasions. At that rate, your business should plan for payment problems as a recurring operating condition.


**Lost revenue** is the easiest part of the cost to see, as the same failed payment also creates


**retry attempts** ,


**customer support tickets** ,


**payment status checks** ,


**refunds** , and


**reconciliation** work. A different team handles each one, and every case takes time your business pays for.


The difference changes what your business fixes. Count only the lost sale, and the obvious answer is a better checkout page. Count the support tickets, refunds, and reconciliation work behind it, and the answer becomes better payment visibility and faster recovery.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- Why a single failed payment reaches your customer, your revenue, and your internal teams at the same time


- The costs that appear after checkout is over, from manual investigation to refunds and reconciliation


- Why a failure rate that looks small in percentage terms becomes material at enterprise transaction volumes


- What your business can control, covering detection, automatic recovery, customer recovery options, and connected payment records


- How Xendit supports each of those through reliability, webhook recovery, payment status visibility, refunds, and local payment method coverage


The costs of payment failures arrive in two waves, and the first one hits while the customer is still at checkout.


## **What happens to your business when a payment fails**


A failed payment affects three parts of your business at the same time:


- **Your customer** , who may abandon the purchase or try to pay again


- **Your revenue** , which loses an order you already spent money to win


- **Your internal teams** , who have to confirm what happened to the money and resolve it


All three can be affected within minutes of a single failed payment attempt.


**The immediate impact is a lost or delayed conversion**


When a customer cannot complete a payment, the most immediate consequence is a purchase that either stalls or moves elsewhere. Visa found that


[47% of Asia Pacific respondents](https://www.visa.com.sg/about-visa/stories/2025/commerce-of-tomorrow-why-ecommerce-growth-in-asia-pacific-depends-on-frictionless-secure-payments.html) would visit another merchant or abandon their purchase after encountering card issues at checkout.


These are customers who already decided to buy, and your business already spent marketing and acquisition budget to get them to your checkout page. At enterprise scale, even a low failure percentage may turn into thousands of orders lost at the final step of the transaction.


***Also read:***[How Payment Success Rates Turn Checkout Demand Into E-Commerce Revenue](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-payment-success-rates-turn-checkout-demand-into-e-commerce-revenue/)


### **Customers try to pay again, which creates duplicate transactions**


A customer who does not see a clear confirmation of whether the payment went through will often try to pay again. For your business, this creates a second transaction record that someone has to match against the first payment attempt before you ship anything or issue a refund.


The difficulty is that three different payment states can produce the same complaint from a customer, so your team has to identify which one the transaction is actually in:


- A payment that failed, where no money left the customer's account


- A payment still waiting for confirmation from the bank or wallet provider


- A payment that succeeded, where the confirmation reached your system late


The right payment infrastructure makes these three payment states easy to tell apart. Xendit's


[payment status endpoint](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/get-payment) returns a defined status for every transaction, including pending, succeeded, failed, and expired payments, so your systems know which situation they are in before deciding what to show the customer.


The hardest case is a


[delayed webhook](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/delayed-webhooks) , where the payment method provider confirms the payment later than when the customer authorized it. Without a clear view of which payments are still pending, your business can end up collecting payment twice for the same order.


###


### **Payment issues turn into customer support tickets**


Customers contact support when they are unsure whether they were charged or whether the order went through. Your agent has to check the transaction before telling the customer to retry, wait, or expect a refund, and that check has to happen while the customer is still waiting.


The customer usually has one number on hand, which is the receipt reference their bank or wallet app gave them. Xendit returns that


**same identifier** on the payment record, as a


**retrieval reference number** for cards and a


**receipt ID** for other channels, so your agent can find the transaction using the number the customer is reading out.


At


**high transaction volumes** , even a small share of payment-related contacts adds up to a large ticket queue, and the time spent on each one becomes a real cost.


Lost conversion, duplicate attempts, and support tickets are the costs most businesses already count, because all three show up on the same day as the failed payment. The costs that follow after usually do not appear in a checkout report at all.


## **The hidden operational costs behind a failed payment**


Once checkout is over, the work moves to teams who never speak to the customer. These are the


**three operational tasks that create most of the hidden cost of payment failures** for businesses processing high volumes in Southeast Asia:


**Manual investigation when your records and the payment record disagree**


When the payment result your customer saw at checkout and the order status your system recorded do not match, your operations or engineering team has to establish what actually happened to the transaction. That usually means checking the payment status, reviewing webhook events, pulling settlement records, and comparing all three against your order system.


For a transaction that appears in one system and not the other, Xendit's


[transaction reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) sets out the checks to run, covering transaction timing and time zones, webhook delivery logs, and API response codes. Each check is time-consuming, and


**speed** matters here, since a payment problem is much easier to resolve within the first hour than after it has been left open for three days.


**Refunds and reversals that have to be tracked separately**


A refund is a second transaction that has to stay connected to the first. A refund created through


[Xendit's refund API](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/refund-payment-request) is raised against the original payment request, carries its own refund ID, records a reason such as a customer request or a duplicate charge, and moves from pending to succeeded or failed on its own timeline.


For a business operating at scale, that structure is what lets finance


**connect a refund back to the transaction it came from** . Without a shared reference between the two, your team matches refunds to payments by amount and date, which becomes complex and stops being reliable the moment two customers pay the same amount on the same day.


**Reconciliation work created by unclear payment and settlement status**


Failed and ambiguous payments create


**gaps** between your


**payment records** and your


**order records** , and settlement timing widens them.


[Settlement](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) ranges from instant to several business days depending on the payment channel, and for e-wallets, QR payments, direct debit, and PayLater it is counted in calendar days, so a settlement date falling on a weekend moves to the next.


**Delayed or failed callbacks** from banks are one of the most common causes of missing transactions, which is why


**automated reconciliation** runs on a regular cycle and can surface a missing transaction days after the payment during a bank outage. For your finance team, an order marked as “paid” does not tell them when the money arrives, because the payment date and the settlement date can fall in different months.


***Also read:***[The Multi-Entity Reconciliation Guide for Businesses Operating Across Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/the-multi-entity-reconciliation-guide-for-businesses-operating-across-southeast-asia/)


At a few thousand transactions a month, these costs stay small. At enterprise volume, they grow with everything else.


## **Why the cost of payment failures grows at enterprise scale**


Growth in payment volume changes three things about payment failure, and each one adds work your teams did not have to do at lower transaction volumes:


**1. A small failure rate can affect thousands of transactions**


Consider a business processing 1 million payment attempts in a period. If 0.5% of those attempts are affected by a payment issue, that is 5,000 transactions carrying some combination of lost revenue, a support contact, a refund, and a reconciliation exception.


Treat 0.5% as an illustration, since real failure rates vary by market and payment method. What the example shows is why your business should track the number of


**affected transactions** alongside the


**percentage** . In a monthly report, 0.5% looks small enough to ignore. As 5,000 transactions, it becomes a workload your support and finance teams have to clear before the month closes.


**2. More payment methods create more failure scenarios**


**** Southeast Asia's payment mix widens the surface area.


[Mastercard](https://www.mastercard.com/news/ap/en/perspectives/en/2024/tech-trends-and-trust-making-south-east-asia-s-digital-economy-work-for-all/) reported that the region's


**gross transaction value for digital payments** was expected to pass


**US$1 trillion in 2025** , with


**digital wallets** and


**QR code payments** reshaping how customers pay.


For your business, that means running cards, bank transfers, virtual accounts, QR payments, e-wallets, and other local payment methods at the same time, each with its own processing flow, authentication step, and provider.


Each payment method also fails for different reasons, for example, a card can be declined by the issuing bank, an e-wallet payment can fail when the customer's balance is too low, and a virtual account payment can expire before the customer transfers the money.


Xendit returns a


[specific failure code](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/get-payment) on every payment, covering cases such as insufficient balance, an unavailable channel, an expired OTP, a customer who did not authorize the payment, and a decline from the issuing bank. For card payments, Xendit also passes through the


[decline codes returned by the card networks](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) , which give your team more detail on why an issuer refused the transaction. As your payment coverage grows, that detail is what tells your team which method, market, or step in the transaction created the problem.


**3. Operating across several markets makes diagnosis harder**


**** Enterprise businesses operating across Southeast Asia run different payment methods and transaction flows in each market. When an issue appears, your team first has to establish whether it is


**isolated** to one market or one payment channel, or whether it points to something


**broader** in the payment infrastructure.


Answering that question quickly depends on


**centralized visibility** and


**consistent payment event handling** across markets. Without it, each market team investigates separately, reaches its own conclusion, and your business ends up resolving the same incident several times.


***Also read:***[Enterprise Payment Infrastructure for Peak E-Commerce Traffic, A Southeast Asia Guide](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/enterprise-payment-infrastructure-for-peak-e-commerce-traffic-a-southeast-asia-guide/) ******


Transaction volume scale explains why these costs grow. What your business can still control is how quickly each failed payment is detected, recovered, and closed.


## **How to reduce payment failures and recover more transactions at scale**


No payment setup removes failure completely, because part of every transaction depends on a bank, a wallet provider, or the customer's device. What your business controls is what happens next, from how fast a failure is detected to how much of it recovers without anyone touching it.


Below are


**four practices that help your business detect payment failures** faster and


**recover more transactions** across Southeast Asia:


### **1. Detect payment issues quickly**


Your team needs to separate failed, pending, successful, and refunded transactions without having to open a second system. Xendit reports


[transaction status and settlement status](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) as a pair across the


[dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) , API responses, and


[reports](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reports-overview) , so a payment that has been captured but not yet settled reads differently from one that has already reached your balance.


For your business, that pairing prevents a payment that is simply waiting to settle from being reported and investigated as a failed payment.


### **2. Make temporary failures recover on their own**


Temporary failures should not automatically become manual investigations. Xendit retries unsuccessful


[webhook deliveries](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/webhook-behavior) up to six times using exponential backoff, with the final attempt arriving 24 hours after the original event, so payment-status information still reaches your business when the receiving system is briefly unavailable.


How your own system receives those updates matters just as much. Xendit's


[webhook handling](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/handling-webhooks) covers four practices worth building in:


- Check each update against the unique payment ID and capture ID, so the same payment event is never processed twice


- Verify the callback token on every update before acting on it


- Return a success response first and run heavier logic afterward, so your endpoint does not time out


- Hold updates in a queue, since they can arrive out of order


- Each of those removes a category of failure that would otherwise reach your engineering team as a ticket.


### **3. Give customers a way to complete the purchase after a failure**


When one payment attempt fails, customers should be able to retry or choose another available payment method


**while intent is still high** . Your business gets a second chance at the transaction instead of losing the customer entirely.


Uncertain cases need a written process too. While your system waits for confirmation, show the customer a


**pending payment notice** instead of a failure message. When a provider confirms late, ask the customer to


**keep the receipt** from their payment app, hold the order for up to 24 hours, which is the average Xendit


**reconciliation** time, or close the order and refund once settlement arrives.


Putting that in your support team playbook turns an uncertain transaction into a standard flow your agents can follow, so customers keep enough confidence in the purchase to complete it instead of abandoning the order.


**4. Keep payments, refunds, and settlements traceable to one order**


Your team uses two different transaction identifiers for two different jobs, and Xendit's


[reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) separates them clearly. The order reference ID your business generates works as the


**reconciliation ID** , while Xendit's payment ID, plus the capture ID where a payment is captured in parts, works as the


**investigation ID** .


With that split in place, your finance team reconciles using your own order reference ID, while your support and engineering teams raise cases with Xendit using the payment ID. Neither team has to rebuild the link between the two records by hand at month-end.


These four practices depend on what the


**payment infrastructure** underneath produces. That is where the choice of payment partner starts to affect the numbers.

Refund support and the number of partial refunds allowed differ by payment channel, so check the rules for each


[payment method](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) before you publish a refund policy your support team has to apply.


**5. Multiple payment methods as a recovery route**


Supporting several relevant payment methods gives customers another way to complete a purchase when one payment route does not work. Xendit provides access to


[more than 100 payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) across its operating markets through one integration, and channels can be


[activated from the Dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) as your payment data comes in.


This carries particular weight across Southeast Asia, where payment preferences and payment methods differ by market. A customer paying through a method they use daily is less likely to fail in the first place, and an alternative method at checkout converts a failed attempt into a completed order instead of an abandoned one.


For an enterprise processing high transaction volumes across Southeast Asia, one failed payment may become a lost sale, a support interaction, a reconciliation task, or a refund your finance team has to close.


**Payment infrastructure** therefore has to do more than process transactions. It should prevent failures where possible, recover from temporary issues without manual work, and keep payment status clear when something does go wrong, so a failed transaction costs your business one line in a report instead of a week of your teams' time.

## **FAQ for enterprise businesses in Southeast Asia: Payment failures and recovery**


### **How do you tell the difference between a failed payment and one that is only delayed?**


You need a payment status that separates the two, since treating a pending payment as a failure is what leads to double charges and unnecessary refunds.


**Xendit** returns a defined status for every payment through the


[Get Payment endpoint](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/get-payment) , including pending, succeeded, failed, and expired, and sends the same information through webhooks. Your systems can then hold the order, release it, or prompt a retry based on what actually happened.


### **What happens if a customer is charged but your system never receives the confirmation?**


This usually means the payment method provider confirmed the payment later than the customer authenticated it.


**Xendit** documents the handling for this as a


[delayed webhook](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/delayed-webhooks) , covering when to hold the order, when to close it, and when to refund the customer once settlement arrives. Xendit's automated reconciliation also picks up payments a provider failed to report or reported as a failure, so the transaction still reaches your records even when the provider never sent a confirmation.


### **How many times will a payment provider retry a webhook before your team has to step in?**


**Xendit** re-delivers an unsuccessful


[webhook](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/webhook-behavior) up to six times on an exponential backoff schedule, stopping once your server confirms receipt. If your endpoint was unavailable for longer than that window, your team can resend a specific event from the Dashboard or use Custom Retry to resend a filtered batch of missed updates. Recovering from an outage on your side stays inside your operations team instead of becoming a support escalation.


### **Can you issue a partial refund when only part of an order needs to be returned?**


Yes.


**Xendit** supports both full and partial refunds through the


[refund API](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/refund-payment-request) , raised against the original payment request and carrying a reason code your finance team can report on. Availability and the number of partial refunds permitted differ by payment channel, so confirm the rules for each method in the


[available payment channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) directory before you publish your refund policy.


### **How do you find out why a payment failed across different payment methods?**


Cards, e-wallets, QR, and bank payment channels fail for different reasons, so a single failure count will not tell your team what to fix.


**Xendit** returns a specific failure code on every payment, covering cases such as insufficient balance, an unavailable channel, an expired OTP, and a decline from the issuing bank, which separates customer-side causes from channel-side ones. Grouping those codes by market and


[payment method](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) shows where recovery effort earns the most back.


### **How do you reconcile payments when the transaction date and the settlement date fall in different months?**


Your reports need both dates on the same record, since a payment captured at the end of one month can settle in the next.


**Xendit** reports


[transaction status and settlement status](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) as a pair on every transaction, and


[reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) sets out how to match your own order reference ID against Xendit's payment and capture IDs. Your finance team then reviews the exceptions instead of rebuilding the link between orders, payments, and settlements manually.


### **Does adding more payment methods reduce how many transactions you lose to failures?**


It gives a failed attempt somewhere to go, which is where most of the recovery comes from. When a customer's first method declines and no alternative is available at checkout, the transaction ends there, while a second familiar option turns that attempt into a completed order.


**Xendit** gives your business


[more than 100 payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) across its operating markets through one integration, so your payment mix can match how each Southeast Asian market pays without a separate build per country.
